mainEntity.name: What does a negative z-score mean?

acceptedAnswer.text: It means the value is below the mean. A z-score of −1.5 is one and a half standard deviations below average, which on a normal distribution is about the 6.68th percentile.

mainEntity.name: How do I convert a z-score to a percentile?

acceptedAnswer.text: Evaluate the standard normal cumulative distribution function Φ(z) and multiply by 100. For example Φ(1.00) = 0.8413, so z = 1 is the 84.13th percentile. This calculator does that for you and also shows both tail areas.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a z-score and a t-score?

acceptedAnswer.text: A z-score uses a known population standard deviation and the normal distribution. A t statistic uses a standard deviation estimated from a small sample and the t distribution, which has heavier tails. Separately, "T-score" in psychometrics means a standardised score with mean 50 and standard deviation 10, which is unrelated to the t distribution.

mainEntity.name: What are the critical z-values for 95% and 99% confidence?

acceptedAnswer.text: For a two-sided interval, z = 1.960 for 95% confidence and z = 2.576 for 99% confidence. For 90% it is 1.645. Use the inverse mode with a percentile of 97.5 or 99.5 to reproduce them.

mainEntity.name: Should I use the sample or the population standard deviation?

acceptedAnswer.text: Use the population standard deviation (divide by N) only when your data is the whole population. If it is a sample drawn from a larger group, divide by n − 1 to get the unbiased estimate of the variance, which is the usual choice.

mainEntity.name: Does the percentile work for any data?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The z-score itself is always valid, but the percentile and tail areas assume an approximately normal distribution. For strongly skewed or heavy-tailed data they can be badly off.
